newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota warns it is leaning away from Britain.
newsitem.headline: Toyota warns it is leaning away from Britain.

text.p: Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda on Wednesday seemed to rule out further investment in the near future by the carmaker in Britain, and warned the company would turn all its attention to the Continent if London stayed out of European monetary union.

In comments that could turn into an issue in Britain's forthcoming general election campaign, Okuda left no doubt that a Britain outside the European Economic and Monetary union (EMU) was of little interest to the giant carmaker.
"Regardless on whether Britain joins (the EMU), I have a feeling that it would be excessive if we made additional (investments) in Britain," Okuda told reporters.
Okuda said that Toyota would shift its European investments to continental Europe if Britain did not join the EMU.
In London a spokesman for Prime Minister John Major's Downing Street office reacted quickly, saying: "I am not going to take it at face value."

He added that an announcement last year that Toyota would create around 1,000 jobs through an additional 200 million sterling ($323.9 million) investment to boost capacity at its Derbyshire plant "indicates to me great confidence in the United Kingdom."
Toyota's Okuda was asked if the carmaker's future strategy in Britain would change, depending on whether the UK joined the EMU, Okuda said, "It will change."
Toyota last year built 117,000 cars at its Derbyshire, central England, plant.

Last week, Britain's main opposition Labour party seized on less forthright comments by a senior Toyota European executive that Toyota was worried that some Conservative "Euro-sceptics" wanted to pull out of the European Union.
"It would be of great concern to Toyota if the UK found itself excluded from the European Union," Alan Marsh, vice-chairman of Toyota Motor Europe, told the Times newspaper.
Asked specifically if Toyota's investment would decrease if Britain opted out of EMU, Okuda said: "Rather than decreasing the amount, we will leave investments as they are now.
"But if we were to make fresh investments, we would prefer to make them in continental Europe rather than Britain," he added.
